articles.title: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind
articles.summary_raw: Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work - I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today's coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions. They're too good at describing the work The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That's a lot of information to absorb. It's not necessarily slop, but it reads like slop! It's very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as "I'm not reading all of that". It doesn't matter how accurate or useful the information is, I'm instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me! I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just long enough about the PR to give me a human-approved introduction that helps me understand, at a high level, what the PR is for and whether it deserves more of my attention. I think I've found a low-effort way to do this that feels right. Hide most of it in a details/summary The HTML <details><summary> elements render as a collapsed heading (the summary) that can be expanded to view the larger piece of text. The code looks like this: < details > < summary > Claude Opus 5.5 </ summary > < h2 > The hook </ h2 > Plugins implement < code > register_agent_reference_types(datasette) </ code > ... </ details > When rendered, it looks like this : Crucially, <details><summary> is supported in GitHub Markdown . You can drop those tags directly into an issue comment or PR description and GitHub will hide the details and display ju…

articles.title: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust
articles.summary_raw: Research: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust I was out walking the dog when I got curious about how easy/difficult it would be to write a SQLite C extension that adds a parse_number() function for turning strings like -$1,234.56 or '12.5%' into numeric values that could be summed and sorted. I fired up regular Claude chat (Opus 5.5) and prompted : I'm thinking about a SQLite custom function 'parse_number(value)' that strips ',', '$', '£' and '%', handles a leading '-', and returns 'NULL' for anything it can’t parse Explore the difference between building this as a SQLite extension in C v.s. in Rust - I want to compare performance and code complexity and size of the resulting .so (or whatever) file This gave me a solid starting point - the Rust extension was 321 KB (using Rusqlite ) and 298 KB (using sqlite-loadable-rs ), while the C extension was 14 KB. But the Rust extension was faster! Turns out that's because the Rust equivalent of C's strtod is "twice as fast". So I prompted: Try writing your own C function for parsing text into a decimal number that catches up to or beats the Rust implementation And it did: Net cost per row over 2 million rows, lower is better: first C new C rusqlite sqlite-loadable Mixed data 67 ns 19 ns 46 ns 41 ns Integers only 25 ns 16 ns 36 ns 32 ns Decimals only 106 ns 18 ns 55 ns 47 ns Finally, I had it rewrite the prototype as a research report to match the others in simonw/research by prompting this: Clone simonw/research from GitHub and turn your above investigation into a research report as seen in that repository - you can give me a zip file to download that contains your new folder Here's the resulting report . Tags: c , research , sqlite , rust , claude

articles.title: datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages
articles.summary_raw: datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages I was looking at the Firefox network panel today when I noticed that requests to a Datasette table page were triggering an HTTP prefetch to the next page of rows in that table. This was happening because Datasette pages serve an HTTP link header like this: link: <https://latest.datasette.io/fixtures/compound_three_primary_keys?_next=a%2Cd%2Cv>; rel="next" This is bad. A tiny fraction of the visitors to one of those pages will click the "next" link, which means for everyone else their browser is fetching unnecessary data and the Datasette server is having to render an entire page that then gets thrown away. I dug in and learned that Firefox has an issue that has been open for 24 years about this behavior... And one of the early comments on that issue links to my blog post from 2002 complaining about this feature. I hadn't just forgotten that I had written about it, I had forgotten the feature entirely! Tags: firefox , html , mozilla , datasette

articles.title: Terry Pratchett's Study
articles.summary_raw: My comment on Terry Pratchett's Study — Hacker News. Terry Pratchett once wrote about the concept of "horizontal wealth". Vertical wealth is where you spend money on rich people stuff - yachts and suchlike. Horizontal wealth is where you spend more money on the things you liked before you got rich: https://chibuikeani.blogspot.com/2017/02/the-price-of-happin... But horizontal wealth means not letting your increased income dictate your tastes. You like books and now you have money? Buy more books! Change those catenary bookshelves for good hardwood ones! In my case, build a library extension to your office. And, of course, you buy what will be useful for that most wonderful of pursuits, blind research, which is research without direction for the sheer joy of it. (Original source is his book A Slip of the Keyboard - this linked blog post quotes that bit.) Tags: hacker-news , terry-pratchett
